extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in ACLU history and civil liberties
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive historical account of the American Civil Liberties Union's activities, policies, controversies, and internal debates across the 20th and 21st centuries. Covers litigation, policy positions, internal memos, affiliate relations, and public criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for deciding whether to take a case (internal memo, June 2018)
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal ACLU memo dated June 2018 discussed factors to evaluate when deciding whether to take a case, listing several factors to consider, including "the extent to which the speech may assist in advancing the goals of white supremacists or others whose views are contrary to our values."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo's authors stated the memo did not define a change in official ACLU policy but was intended as a guideline to assist ACLU affiliates in deciding which cases to take. The document thus functions as an internal decision-guideline (case-selection criteria), weighing potential harms such as assisting extremist goals against free-speech principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of defending free speech even when repulsive
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU stated: "it is easy to defend freedom of speech when the message is something many people find at least reasonable. But the defense of freedom of speech is most critical when the message is one most people find repulsive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an articulated normative standard guiding case choice and public defense: prioritize protection of speech rights especially for unpopular or repulsive viewpoints. Historically applied in controversies (e.g., defending Nazi marchers in Skokie, defending NRA speech) and used to explain why the organization sometimes defends deeply unpopular speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Security Project policy standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU's National Security Project advocates for national security policies that are "consistent with the Constitution, the rule of law, and fundamental human rights." The Project litigates cases relating to detention, torture, discrimination, surveillance, censorship, and secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy sets a substantive evaluative standard for national-security–related litigation and advocacy: any national security policy or practice should be assessed for consistency with constitutional protections, rule-of-law principles, and human-rights norms. Examples in the text include litigation over detention programs, surveillance, and post-9/11 measures; the policy statement frames what kinds of national-security issues the ACLU prioritizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational voting rule permitting affiliate participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolutions were the first to fall under the ACLU's new organizational rules permitting local affiliates to participate in the vote; the affiliates outvoted the national headquarters and rejected the anti-communist resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule is a governance criterion that affects policy decisions: allowing affiliate participation changes how organizational policy is decided and can override national office positions. It functions as a structural standard for legitimacy and internal decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-selection and priority influenced by donor and membership considerations (criticized practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff members privately protested that quixotic, high-profile initiatives were displacing essential, low-profile work, and reported being discouraged or prevented from working on cases or controversies unpopular with ACLU members and (especially) major donors, or merely unlikely to inspire substantial contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While presented as criticism, this describes an implicit criterion (or anti-pattern) shaping which cases the organization pursues: perceived donor preferences and fundraising potential can influence case acceptance and priority-setting. It functions as a caution about non-legal factors affecting organizational decisions.
